questions.question: A Deployment manages 3 replicas of a Pod. A node running one replica fails permanently. What restores the desired replica count?
options: The kubelet on the failed node restarts the Pod locally
The ReplicaSet controller creates a replacement Pod, which the scheduler places on a healthy node
kube-proxy migrates the Pod's network identity to another node
The container runtime re-pulls the image on the failed node
questions.explanation: The ReplicaSet controller (managed by the Deployment) notices the missing replica and creates a new Pod; the scheduler then assigns it to a schedulable node.

questions.question: Which component decides which node a newly created, unscheduled Pod runs on?
options: kube-apiserver
kubelet
kube-scheduler
etcd
questions.explanation: kube-scheduler watches for Pods with no assigned node and binds them to a suitable node based on resource requests, affinity, taints, and other constraints.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a container image and a running container?
options: An image includes the kernel; a container does not
An image is an immutable, layered filesystem plus metadata; a container is a running instance with a writable layer
Images run in the cloud while containers run locally
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Images are immutable templates. Starting one creates a container: the image layers plus a writable layer and an isolated process namespace, sharing the host kernel.

questions.question: Which statements about namespaces are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: They can scope resource quotas and RBAC permissions
They provide hard network isolation by default
Some cluster-level resources, such as Nodes, are not namespaced
Deleting a namespace deletes the namespaced resources inside it
questions.explanation: Namespaces scope quotas, RBAC, and object names, and deleting one removes its contents. They do NOT isolate network traffic by default — that requires NetworkPolicies.

questions.question: In the Kubernetes network model, which requirement must every cluster network implementation satisfy?
options: Every Pod gets its own IP address and can reach every other Pod without NAT
All Pods share the node's IP address
Pods can only communicate through Services
Cross-node Pod traffic must go through the API server
questions.explanation: The flat Pod network model gives each Pod a unique IP and requires Pod-to-Pod reachability without NAT; CNI plugins implement this.

questions.question: A Pod needs storage that survives Pod restarts and rescheduling to another node. Which combination provides that?
options: An emptyDir volume
A hostPath volume
A PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a network-backed PersistentVolume
Container-local scratch space
questions.explanation: emptyDir dies with the Pod, hostPath is tied to one node. A PVC bound to a network-backed PV survives rescheduling because the storage is independent of any node.

questions.question: Which mechanism grants a Pod's workload an identity for authenticating to the Kubernetes API?
options: A NodePort Service
A ServiceAccount token mounted into the Pod
The container image digest
An Ingress annotation
questions.explanation: Pods run as a ServiceAccount; a projected token gives the workload an identity that RBAC rules can authorize.

questions.question: What best describes the GitOps delivery model?
options: Developers apply manifests manually with kubectl after each merge
A CI server pushes images directly into running Pods
The desired state lives in Git, and an in-cluster agent continuously reconciles the cluster toward it
Operators SSH into nodes to update workloads
questions.explanation: GitOps treats Git as the source of truth; tools like Argo CD or Flux watch the repo and reconcile the cluster to match it, giving auditable, declarative delivery.

questions.question: Which three signals are commonly called the pillars of observability?
options: Metrics, logs, and traces
Alerts, dashboards, and reports
CPU, memory, and disk
Uptime, latency, and cost
questions.explanation: Metrics (numeric time series), logs (event records), and traces (request paths across services) are the classic observability pillars; OpenTelemetry standardizes collecting them.

questions.question: Which statement about the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) is correct?
options: It resizes the CPU and memory limits of existing Pods
It adds or removes Pod replicas based on observed metrics such as CPU utilization
It adds new nodes to the cluster when capacity runs out
It only works with DaemonSets
questions.explanation: HPA scales replica counts of Deployments/ReplicaSets/StatefulSets from metrics. Resizing Pod resources is the Vertical Pod Autoscaler; adding nodes is the Cluster Autoscaler.
